chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
## The Benchmark Deal

In June 2025, Talen Energy Supply signed an expansion of its power purchase agreement with Amazon Web Services that repositioned a mid-sized Pennsylvania independent power producer at the centre of the most consequential structural shift in US electricity markets in a generation. Under the amended contract, Talen agreed to deliver up to 1,920 megawatts of carbon-free nuclear baseload from its Susquehanna Steam Electric Station through 2042 — among the largest single carbon-free data centre PPAs in US history, and the transaction that effectively set the market price for AI electricity sourced directly from nuclear.

Talen Energy Corporation (TLN, NASDAQ) is headquartered in Houston, though its generation identity is firmly Pennsylvanian. The company holds 13.1 gigawatts of US capacity: 2.2 GW nuclear (a 90% ownership stake in the 2.5 GW Susquehanna facility in Luzerne County), 5.7 GW of low- and zero-carbon baseload in aggregate, 2.8 GW of natural gas combined-cycle acquired through the Freedom and Guernsey transactions closed in fiscal year 2025, and 4.6 GW of intermediate and peaking capacity, alongside roughly 800 MW in minority coal interests.

Chief Executive Mark "Mac" McFarland, who joined Talen in May 2023, arrived with the precise biography the role demanded: senior vice president at Exelon, chief commercial officer at Energy Future Holdings and Luminant, executive chairman and CEO at GenOn Energy — a career built almost entirely inside post-restructuring power companies navigating the intersection of commodity markets and regulated assets. Chairman Stephen Schaefer carries a complementary pedigree from Riverstone Holdings, the GenOn Holdings board, and Golar LNG. The company itself emerged from Chapter 11 in 2023 and relisted on NASDAQ — a trajectory that shaped both its capital structure discipline and its appetite for large-scale contracted revenue.

## Generation Economics

The financial logic of Talen's position rests on a single arithmetic fact: Susquehanna generated approximately 17 terawatt-hours in fiscal year 2025 at an implied levelised cost of roughly $27 per megawatt-hour. That figure places Susquehanna among the most economic large baseload assets on the PJM interconnection, whose footprint stretches from New Jersey to Illinois. Selling that output into spot markets would be profitable; selling it to a hyperscaler at PPA contract prices over a seventeen-year term is structurally different — it converts a commodity asset into something closer to a regulated utility cash flow, with none of the regulated utility's return constraints.

Fiscal year 2025 delivered $1,035 million of adjusted EBITDA and $524 million of adjusted free cash flow — a conversion ratio of approximately 50%, which is strong for an IPP carrying the maintenance capital obligations of an operating nuclear facility and a fleet of gas-fired plants across multiple PJM zones.

## Contracted Revenue Layers

The Amazon PPA is the headline, but it sits atop a more complex revenue architecture. Talen cleared 8,745 MW in PJM's 2027/2028 capacity auction at $333.44 per MW-day — a clearing price that, applied across that volume, implies roughly $1.06 billion of annual capacity payments at that auction level. Separately, the company holds reliability must-run contracts on two Maryland coal facilities: Brandon Shores ($145 million per year) and H.A. Wagner ($35 million per year), both running through May 2029. Together the RMR contracts contribute $180 million of fixed annual revenue regardless of market conditions.

The layering — nuclear PPA, capacity auction, RMR — is deliberate architecture rather than coincidence. It reflects an executive team that emerged from EFH and GenOn with a precise understanding of how revenue-stack construction insulates an IPP's free-cash-flow base from commodity price cycles.

## The Acquisition Wager

The larger strategic bet is in gas. Talen closed the Freedom and Guernsey combined-cycle acquisitions during fiscal year 2025 for approximately $3.8 billion, adding 2.8 GW of dispatchable gas capacity to the fleet. The pending Cornerstone transaction, agreed at approximately $3.45 billion, would contribute a further 2.0 GW of combined-cycle plus 456 MW of peaking. The total programme — roughly $7.25 billion for approximately 5.3 GW — has been financed in part through $1.4 billion of 6.250% senior unsecured notes due 2034 and $1.3 billion of 6.500% notes due 2036, with management targeting net leverage around 3.5 times or lower across the cycle.

The central tension that defines the investment case is straightforward to state and difficult to resolve. AI data centre electricity demand has already repriced PJM baseload in ways observable in both the Amazon PPA structure and the 2027/2028 capacity auction clearing prices. Talen sits at the intersection of nuclear monetisation, gas-capacity consolidation, RMR contracts, and capacity-market optionality in a single listed vehicle. Whether the AI capital expenditure cycle sustains long enough — and at sufficient electricity intensity — for those contracted layers and the gas acquisition programme to compound into a materially larger free-cash-flow base is the question that will determine whether the premium embedded in TLN's NASDAQ valuation proves justified or premature.

chapters.title: From PPL spin-off to AI electricity supplier
chapters.body:
## The spin-off that Riverstone took private

Talen Energy was assembled, not born. In 2015 PPL Corporation, the Pennsylvania utility holding company, separated its competitive generation business and combined it with the merchant-power portfolio held by Riverstone Holdings, the New York private-equity firm that had spent the prior decade accumulating unregulated generation assets across PJM and the mid-Atlantic. The resulting company — Talen Energy Corporation — began life as a publicly listed independent power producer with a multi-state fleet anchored by the 2.5-gigawatt Susquehanna Steam Electric Station in Luzerne County, Pennsylvania, one of the largest boiling-water reactor complexes in the eastern United States.

The IPO window was brief. By 2016 Riverstone had concluded that the public-market valuation on offer for unregulated generation was insufficient and took Talen private in a leveraged buyout. The decision reflected a broader tension in the IPP sector: wholesale electricity prices in PJM had fallen sharply through the mid-2010s as shale-gas production drove natural gas prices toward structural lows and as renewable-capacity additions — subsidised by federal tax credits — steadily expanded the supply stack. The merchant-power model that had looked attractive at the top of the commodity cycle increasingly resembled a leveraged short on fuel prices.

For Talen, the consequence of private ownership through this period was a capital structure calibrated to the optimism of 2016 colliding with a half-decade of compressed power-price realizations. The combination of the 2020 COVID demand collapse, the Ukraine-driven commodity spike in 2022, and the hedging and refinancing constraints that followed produced a balance sheet that could no longer support its debt load.

## Chapter 11 and the NASDAQ relisting

Talen Energy filed for Chapter 11 protection in 2022. The restructuring eliminated a substantial portion of the pre-petition debt, shed non-core obligations, and refocused the portfolio around the Susquehanna nuclear asset and the company's remaining gas and coal positions in PJM. In 2023 the company emerged from bankruptcy with a restructured balance sheet and completed a new public listing on NASDAQ under the ticker TLN — a comparatively fast passage from filing to relisting that reflected both the quality of the nuclear asset and the clarity of the restructuring thesis.

The CEO appointment that followed set the tone for everything that came after. Mark "Mac" McFarland joined as Chief Executive Officer in May 2023, carrying a career that reads as a map of every major post-Chapter-11 energy restructuring in the United States over the prior two decades: Senior Vice President at Exelon, Chief Commercial Officer at both Luminant and Energy Future Holdings — the Texas merchant giant whose 2014 bankruptcy was the largest in US power-sector history — then Executive Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of GenOn Energy, itself a restructured IPP, and then Chief Executive Officer of California Resources Corporation, the oil and gas producer that also emerged from Chapter 11. McFarland holds a Civil Engineering degree from Virginia Tech, an MBA from the University of Delaware, and has completed the MIT Nuclear Reactor Technology course — a credential whose specificity is not accidental when the asset being run includes 2.25 gigawatts of operating nuclear capacity.

## Building the team from the EFH and GenOn alumni network

The executive team McFarland assembled over the following eighteen months drew heavily from the same restructuring-seasoned talent cluster. Andrew Wright joined as Chief Administrative Officer, bringing fourteen years as General Counsel of Energy Future Holdings — the deepest single EFH institutional memory on the executive floor. Darren Olagues, who had served as CFO and Senior Advisor at GenOn Energy, joined as Chief Development Officer in October 2024. Brad Berryman, already inside the company as Chief Nuclear Officer, was elevated to Chief Operating Officer, bringing thirty years of nuclear plant management experience across Turkey Point, Wolf Creek, and Palo Verde, supplemented by US Navy submarine service — the standard pedigree for senior nuclear-operations executives in the American fleet. Edward Casulli, as Senior Vice President and Chief Nuclear Officer, carried the most site-specific credential of all: prior Site Vice President at Susquehanna itself.

The board assembled above this management layer was constructed with equal deliberation. Stephen Schaefer, the Independent Chairman, came from Riverstone and carries board seats at GenOn Holdings and Golar LNG. Joseph Nigro — Risk Oversight Committee Chair — is the most senior single energy-finance figure on the board: former CFO of Exelon, former Chief Executive of Constellation Energy, and currently Senior Advisor to the Blackstone Energy Transition Group. Anthony Horton, the former Chief Financial Officer of Energy Future Holdings, chairs the Compensation Committee and brings the quadruple finance certification stack — CPA, CFA, CMA, CFM — that EFH's complexity demanded. Karen Hyde, Audit Committee Chair, spent thirty years at Xcel Energy as Chief Compliance and Ethics Officer after beginning her career as a nuclear engineer at the US Department of Defense; she is the NRC-regulatory and compliance specialist by design. Gizman Abbas, Nominating and Governance Committee Chair, carries Apollo Global Management, Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, and ExxonMobil credentials alongside a current board seat at the New York Independent System Operator. Christine Benson Schwartzstein completed seventeen years at Goldman Sachs before moving to Apollo Infrastructure Company and Orion Infrastructure Capital — infrastructure-PE pattern recognition calibrated for precisely the M&A cycle Talen was about to execute.

## The Amazon PPA: pricing AI electricity from a nuclear reactor

The transaction that structurally repositioned Talen in the capital markets arrived in March 2024: a power purchase agreement with Amazon Web Services to supply electricity from Susquehanna to an adjacent AWS data center campus under development in Salem Township, Luzerne County, Pennsylvania. The geographic logic was straightforward — the data center site sat effectively adjacent to the transmission interconnect for a 2.5-gigawatt nuclear plant — but the commercial logic was consequential. Talen had found a buyer willing to pay a contracted price for carbon-free baseload electricity generated at an implied cost of approximately $27 per megawatt-hour, selling into a counterparty whose electricity demand was structurally growing rather than cyclically sensitive.

The initial agreement was expanded materially in June 2025. The revised terms extended the contract through 2042 and increased the maximum contracted volume to 1,920 megawatts, with a ramp schedule potentially reaching full volume by 2032 and delivery rights extending to other Amazon facilities across Pennsylvania. The expansion included an option for Talen and Amazon to co-develop Small Modular Reactors within Talen's Pennsylvania footprint — a provision that embeds a technology-development call option in what is otherwise a commodity-supply contract.

The June 2025 expansion, at up to 1,920 MW of carbon-free nuclear power for seventeen years, is among the largest single clean-energy data center PPAs in US history. It converts what had been a merchant nuclear asset — price-exposed to PJM real-time and day-ahead clearing prices — into a long-dated contracted revenue stream denominated against a hyperscaler counterparty whose credit quality and electricity-demand trajectory are both structurally robust.

## Gas fleet expansion and the balance-sheet build

Against the contracted nuclear revenue anchor, Talen executed an accelerated gas-generation acquisition program through 2025. The Freedom and Guernsey combined-cycle plants closed for approximately $3.8 billion, adding 2.8 gigawatts of natural-gas baseload. The Cornerstone acquisition — 2.0 gigawatts of combined-cycle capacity plus 456 megawatts of peaking — was agreed at approximately $3.45 billion and remained pending at the snapshot date.

The total gas-capacity addition programme amounts to approximately 5.3 gigawatts for roughly $7.25 billion — a transaction scale that required new debt capital. Talen issued $1.4 billion of 6.250% senior unsecured notes due 2034 and $1.3 billion of 6.500% senior unsecured notes due 2036, financing the acquisitions while targeting net leverage of approximately 3.5 times or lower over the cycle.

Alongside the M&A program, Talen secured reliability-must-run contracts on the Brandon Shores and H.A. Wagner plants — $145 million and $35 million annually, respectively, commencing June 2025 and running through May 2029 — adding $180 million of fixed annual revenue from the capacity-market mechanism that PJM uses to retain generation it deems reliability-critical. In the 2027/2028 PJM Base Residual Auction, Talen cleared 8,745 megawatts at $333.44 per megawatt-day, implying approximately $1.06 billion in annual capacity revenue at that clearing price.

## The December 2025 management realignment

As the AWS ramp and the gas acquisition programme moved toward execution simultaneously, Talen formalised an operating-and-financial leadership split. Effective December 15, 2025, Terry Nutt — who had held the CFO role — was elevated to President, a recognition of the operational scaling that Freedom, Guernsey, and the pending Cornerstone integration would demand. Cole Muller, who had served as Executive Vice President for Strategic Ventures and Senior Vice President for Cumulus Growth — the internal designation for the data center colocation and hyperscaler-electricity origination business — was named Chief Financial Officer. Muller holds a US Naval Academy commission, a Wharton MBA, and a University of Pennsylvania law degree alongside prior McKinsey associate partner experience; he was, in a meaningful sense, the architect of the data center electricity thesis before becoming the company's CFO.

## The arc from merchant generator to AI electricity infrastructure

By the snapshot date of May 23, 2026, Talen Energy was two and a half years into post-Chapter-11 public-company life and had executed a transformation in each of the dimensions that matter to sophisticated power-sector investors: contracted revenue (the Amazon PPA through 2042), fleet scale (13.1 gigawatts including Freedom and Guernsey), capacity-market position (8,745 megawatts cleared at record auction prices in PJM's most tightened capacity cycle in a decade), and governance depth (a board whose aggregate pedigree spans Riverstone, Apollo, Goldman Sachs, Blackstone, Exelon, Constellation, and Energy Future Holdings).

The Susquehanna asset — generating approximately 17 terawatt-hours annually at roughly $27 per megawatt-hour of implied cost — sits at the intersection of two structural demand cycles that have rarely coincided in the US power market: AI data center electricity load growth demanding low-carbon, always-on baseload supply, and a PJM capacity-market tightening cycle driven by generator retirements, load growth, and interconnection queue congestion. A company built from the deepest post-restructuring talent network in the US IPP universe now holds what may be the most directly exposed position to both cycles simultaneously.

chapters.title: Nuclear, gas, RMR, and the capacity stack
chapters.body:
## The portfolio in outline

When Talen Energy re-listed on NASDAQ in 2023 following its Chapter 11 emergence, it was, at root, a single large nuclear station wrapped in a shell of inherited gas and coal assets. By the close of FY2025, the company had begun to look rather different: a 13.1 gigawatt independent power producer with a layered revenue architecture that combined nuclear baseload, dispatchable gas capacity, reliability-must-run contracts, and PJM capacity-market payments — all oriented toward an AI-electricity thesis that had begun to attract serious institutional capital.

The generation portfolio breaks into four broad layers. Nuclear and other low-to-zero-carbon baseload totals 5.7 GW, anchored almost entirely by the Susquehanna Steam Electric Station. Natural gas combined-cycle capacity stands at 2.8 GW following the closed Freedom and Guernsey acquisitions. Intermediate and peaking capacity accounts for a further 4.6 GW. And at the margin, roughly 800 MW of minority coal interests — a vestigial position inherited from the pre-bankruptcy fleet — rounds out the stack. The coal exposure carries no strategic weight; management has not framed it as a growth vector, and the relevant investment discussion centres on the first three categories.

## Susquehanna: the economic anchor

The Susquehanna Steam Electric Station, sited on the west branch of the Susquehanna River in Luzerne County, Pennsylvania, is the axis around which the entire Talen investment thesis rotates. At 2.5 GW of total installed capacity across two boiling-water reactor units, it is among the largest single nuclear generating facilities in the PJM footprint and one of the more economic baseload assets in the mid-Atlantic grid. Talen owns 90 percent of the facility — approximately 2.25 GW of attributable capacity — with the remaining interest held by an unaffiliated minority party.

In FY2025, Susquehanna generated approximately 17 terawatt-hours of electricity, implying a capacity factor in the low-to-mid-90-percent range consistent with modern large-pressurised and boiling-water reactor operations. On an all-in production cost basis, the implied levelised cost of electricity runs to approximately $27 per megawatt-hour — a figure that positions Susquehanna comfortably below the prevailing PJM energy clearing price and, critically, well below the contract rates achievable under long-term hyperscaler power purchase agreements. The economics of the Amazon PPA, discussed below, rest fundamentally on that spread.

The regulatory life of the facility extends well into the 2050s. Nuclear Regulatory Commission operating licences for both units provide decades of remaining runway, and the Inflation Reduction Act's nuclear production tax credit — available to existing nuclear generators at $15 per MWh through 2032 and thereafter subject to extension — adds a further layer of cash-flow enhancement not fully reflected in the raw $27/MWh production cost figure. The combination of low marginal cost, long licence life, and federal subsidy support makes Susquehanna structurally irreplaceable within the portfolio.

## Pricing AI electricity: the Amazon PPA

The commercial inflection point for Talen arrived in March 2024, when the company signed an initial power purchase agreement with Amazon Web Services to supply carbon-free nuclear electricity from the Susquehanna campus to an AWS data centre adjacent to the plant site. That initial agreement was expanded materially in June 2025, bringing the contracted volume to up to 1,920 MW of carbon-free baseload capacity — deliverable to the Susquehanna-adjacent AWS campus and to other Amazon-designated sites within Pennsylvania. The term runs through 2042, with a ramp schedule that could reach the full 1,920 MW volume by approximately 2032.

The contract is, by the measure available at the time of the snapshot, among the largest single carbon-free data centre PPAs executed in the United States. The precise contracted price per megawatt-hour is not publicly disclosed in Talen's SEC filings. What is disclosed — and what is economically decisive — is the structural gap between the ~$27/MWh all-in production cost at Susquehanna and the hyperscaler-PPA contract rate, which market observers and industry coverage have consistently characterised as materially above prevailing PJM energy prices. That spread, held for eighteen years, is the core value creation mechanism of the nuclear-to-hyperscaler strategy.

The agreement also contemplates a longer-horizon option: Talen and Amazon are exploring the co-development of small modular reactors within Talen's Pennsylvania generating footprint. SMR co-development remains speculative at the snapshot date, but its inclusion in the disclosed agreement structure signals that both parties view the relationship as a potential decades-long capital partnership rather than a commodity supply contract.

## Firming the baseload: Freedom, Guernsey, and Cornerstone

Nuclear baseload, whatever its economic advantages, is not alone sufficient to serve hyperscaler demand. Data centre loads are continuous and must be matched across all weather conditions and dispatch cycles. Susquehanna's planned and unplanned outage windows — as well as the incremental demand that will ramp under the Amazon contract through 2032 — create a structural need for dispatchable firming capacity. The 2025 gas acquisition programme was the board's answer.

The Freedom and Guernsey facilities, acquired in FY2025 for approximately $3.8 billion, together add 2.8 GW of natural gas combined-cycle capacity to the Talen fleet. Both plants operate in PJM, geographically proximate to the Susquehanna anchor. Combined-cycle gas units — by definition capable of sustained baseload-adjacent operation at high efficiency — are well suited to filling generation gaps in a portfolio anchored by a plant that runs continuously but not perfectly. The scale of the transaction, at $3.8 billion for 2.8 GW, implies a per-kilowatt acquisition cost roughly consistent with the replacement cost of comparable installed gas generation, though the strategic premium is the PJM location and the near-term capacity market positioning.

The Cornerstone transaction, agreed but not yet closed at the snapshot date, adds a further 2.0 GW of combined-cycle capacity alongside 456 MW of peaking generation, for a total consideration of approximately $3.45 billion. The peaking component is economically distinct from the combined-cycle base: peaking units — typically open-cycle gas turbines — are designed to run at high margins for short intervals during demand spikes rather than at continuous baseload. Taken together, the Freedom, Guernsey, and Cornerstone transactions expand Talen's gas-fired installed base by roughly 5.3 GW and total approximately $7.25 billion of committed acquisition capital.

| Acquisition | Capacity | Type | Value | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Freedom + Guernsey | 2.8 GW | Gas combined-cycle | $3.8B | Closed FY2025 |
| Cornerstone | 2.0 GW CC + 456 MW peaking | Gas combined-cycle + peaking | $3.45B | Agreed |
| **Total** | **~5.3 GW** | | **~$7.25B** | |

## The RMR layer: keeping the lights on for a fee

Alongside the nuclear and gas merchant stack, two reliability-must-run contracts provide a categorically different form of revenue stability. RMR designations are issued by PJM to generating facilities that are uneconomic in the capacity market under normal conditions but whose continued operation is required to maintain grid reliability in their local area. Rather than allowing such plants to retire — and risk voltage instability or thermal overload on local transmission — PJM's tariff framework allows it to pay generators a fixed compensation to remain available.

Talen holds RMR contracts on two legacy coal facilities: Brandon Shores and H.A. Wagner, both in the Baltimore area of Maryland. Brandon Shores carries an annual RMR payment of $145 million; H.A. Wagner receives $35 million per year. Both contracts commenced in June 2025 and run through May 2029, locking in a combined $180 million of annual fixed revenue over four years. That $180 million represents a meaningful contribution to cash-flow visibility that sits entirely outside the merchant energy and capacity markets — it is paid regardless of dispatch, regardless of power prices, and regardless of whether competing generation undercuts Talen's bid stack.

The RMR structure is worth understanding precisely because it is not a conventional power contract. The generator is being compensated not for electricity it produces but for reliability optionality it holds. From a credit-quality perspective, the counterparty is effectively PJM Interconnection's tariff — backstopped by the broader pool of load-serving entities in the Mid-Atlantic footprint. The $180 million annual payment flow is, in this sense, among the most structurally secure revenue streams in the Talen stack.

## PJM capacity markets: the revenue ceiling expands

The third major non-Amazon revenue layer is PJM's annual capacity auction, which requires load-serving entities to procure commitments from generation resources sufficient to cover projected peak demand plus a reliability reserve margin. Capacity commitments pay generators a fixed dollar-per-megawatt-day fee in exchange for an obligation to be available during peak conditions.

In the 2027/2028 delivery-year auction — the most recent Talen disclosed at the snapshot date — the company cleared 8,745 MW of capacity at a clearing price of $333.44 per megawatt-day. At that clearing price, 8,745 MW of cleared capacity implies roughly $1.06 billion of annual capacity payments for the delivery year. That figure is not additive to energy revenues in a simple sense — capacity commitments carry physical delivery obligations and opportunity cost constraints — but it represents a substantial and multi-year-visible revenue line that complements the nuclear energy margin and the RMR contracts.

The record 2027/2028 clearing price of $333.44/MW-day — elevated relative to earlier auction cycles by load growth from data centre demand, retirements of uneconomic coal and gas capacity, and PJM's tightening reserve margin outlook — reflects the same structural demand pressures that made the Amazon PPA commercially achievable. Talen, by virtue of its 8.7-GW cleared position and its nuclear-plus-gas stack, is among the primary beneficiaries of that tightening.

## A layered architecture

Viewed as a system, the Talen capacity stack as of FY2025 is a deliberately layered revenue architecture:

| Revenue layer | Approximate scale | Contract/market structure | Term |
|---|---|---|---|
| Amazon AWS PPA (nuclear energy) | Up to 1,920 MW | Long-term bilateral PPA | Through 2042 |
| PJM capacity payments | 8,745 MW cleared | Annual capacity auction (2027/28 prices) | Multi-year via auctions |
| RMR contracts (Brandon Shores + H.A. Wagner) | $180M/year | Fixed-fee reliability contract | Through May 2029 |
| Merchant energy (gas + nuclear residual) | Portfolio-wide | PJM spot + bilateral | Rolling |

The coal minority interests — approximately 800 MW of attributable capacity — sit outside this architecture in any meaningful strategic sense. They are carried positions, generating modest cash flows, whose value to the equity rests primarily in optionality around plant retirement and, conceivably, RMR designation if grid conditions in their service areas deteriorate further.

What the architecture as a whole reveals is a management team that has systematically reduced dependence on any single revenue channel. The $27/MWh nuclear production cost against hyperscaler-PPA contract prices provides energy margin. The $1.06 billion implied capacity payment layer provides a reliability-service revenue base. The $180 million RMR layer provides fixed income regardless of market conditions. And the $524 million of FY2025 adjusted free cash flow — a 50 percent conversion ratio on $1.035 billion of adjusted EBITDA — confirms that the architecture is already generating cash at scale, before the Cornerstone acquisition closes and before the Amazon contract ramps to its 1,920 MW ceiling.

chapters.title: $1,035M EBITDA and the $7.25B acquisition program
chapters.body:
## A Year That Reframed the IPP Category

Fiscal year 2025 closed a chapter on what Talen Energy had been — a reorganised Pennsylvania power producer emerging from bankruptcy — and opened an argument about what it might become. Adjusted EBITDA of $1,035 million against adjusted free cash flow of $524 million produced a cash-conversion ratio of precisely 50%, a figure that analysts covering independent power producers treat as a threshold separating capital-intensive generation businesses from genuinely cash-generative ones. For a company that had exited Chapter 11 less than two years earlier, the headline numbers signalled something more than recovery. They signalled structural repositioning.

The $1,035 million figure sits atop a 13.1-gigawatt portfolio that, in its composition, differs substantially from the mid-2010s vintage IPP playbook. The nuclear anchor at Susquehanna, the RMR contracts on the Maryland coast, the record PJM capacity-auction clearance, and the nascent Amazon PPA revenue layer do not move together with gas spot prices in the way that an unhedged gas-weighted fleet would. That layering — contracted, regulated-adjacent, and merchant, weighted toward the first two — is the architectural choice that informed both the $7.25 billion acquisition program and the capital structure assembled to fund it.

## The Susquehanna Economic Engine

The arithmetic of Susquehanna Station is stark. Talen's 90% ownership share of the 2.5-gigawatt facility generated approximately 17 terawatt-hours in fiscal 2025, at an implied levelised cost of electricity of roughly $27 per megawatt-hour. The production cost basis for the year was therefore approximately $459 million — a figure that includes fuel, operations, maintenance, and nuclear decommissioning trust contributions but not the capital cost of the plant, which was written down through the bankruptcy process and now sits on the balance sheet at reorganisation value rather than replacement cost.

That $27 per megawatt-hour cost basis is not an abstraction. It represents one of the most competitive electricity generation cost structures on the PJM interconnection, a grid spanning thirteen Mid-Atlantic and Midwestern states that dispatches power in economic merit order. In a market where new gas combined-cycle capacity prices at $50 to $70 per megawatt-hour all-in, and where new solar-plus-storage in the region runs higher still, Susquehanna occupies a position of structural advantage that compounds as carbon constraints tighten.

The Amazon Power Purchase Agreement, initially signed in March 2024 and expanded in June 2025, converts that cost advantage into contracted revenue. The June 2025 expansion brought the agreement to up to 1,920 megawatts of carbon-free baseload power, delivered to an Amazon data center campus adjacent to the Susquehanna site in northeastern Pennsylvania and to other facilities in the state, through 2042 — a tenor of roughly seventeen years from the expansion date. The ramp to full contracted volume extends to approximately 2032, reflecting the physical buildout of the campus and interconnection constraints. Talen has not disclosed the per-megawatt-hour contract price. Industry benchmarks for hyperscaler carbon-free baseload PPAs in the Mid-Atlantic region at the time of execution placed comparable agreements in a range of $80 to $120 per megawatt-hour. Even at the low end of that range, the spread against a $27 per megawatt-hour cost basis implies a material and durable EBITDA contribution that will grow as contracted volumes ramp.

The two companies also announced exploration of co-development of small modular reactors within Talen's Pennsylvania footprint — a long-dated optionality that does not figure in near-term financial projections but signals the depth of the commercial relationship and Amazon's stated preference for co-location with zero-carbon generation rather than renewable-energy-certificate-backed offsite agreements.

## Three Revenue Layers Above the Merchant Base

Independent power producers that depend entirely on energy market clearing prices carry earnings volatility that makes debt markets and equity investors price in a risk premium. Talen's revenue architecture, as it stood at the fiscal year 2025 close, rested on three contracted or quasi-contracted layers stacked above whatever commodity price the residual fleet earns in the spot market.

The first layer is the Reliability Must-Run contracts on Brandon Shores and H.A. Wagner, two coal units on the Chesapeake Bay in Maryland that PJM identified as critical for local reliability. The RMR agreements, which took effect in June 2025 and run through May 2029, pay Talen $145 million annually for Brandon Shores and $35 million annually for H.A. Wagner — a combined $180 million per year in fixed revenue regardless of power prices. Across the four remaining years of the contracts at the snapshot date, that represents $720 million of cumulative guaranteed revenue from a grid operator with the balance sheet of the federal government behind it. Management has characterised these plants as candidates for eventual decommissioning or conversion, but through 2029 they function as annuity cash flows.

The second layer is capacity market revenue from PJM's Base Residual Auction. In the 2027/2028 delivery-year auction, Talen cleared 8,745 megawatts at a record clearing price of $333.44 per megawatt-day — a price that reflected tight reserve margins in PJM following years of premature retirements and demand growth driven in part by data center loads in Northern Virginia. At that price and volume, the annualised capacity revenue stream from the 2027/2028 year amounts to approximately $1.06 billion. Capacity payments do not cover fuel or variable operating costs, but they provide revenue certainty well in advance of the delivery period and allow Talen to underwrite fixed costs across the fleet with greater precision than energy-market revenue alone would permit.

The third and structurally most significant layer is the Amazon PPA. Its contribution in fiscal 2025 reflected only the first year of a ramp that will build toward 1,920 megawatts of contracted delivery by approximately 2032. As that volume grows, it will progressively convert Susquehanna's merchant exposure into long-term contracted revenue at prices substantially above current spot power in PJM.

| Revenue Layer | Annual Run Rate | Tenor / Term |
|---|---|---|
| RMR (Brandon Shores + H.A. Wagner) | $180M | Through May 2029 |
| PJM Capacity (2027/28 delivery year) | ~$1,060M | Annual auction cycle |
| Amazon PPA (ramping to 1,920 MW) | Undisclosed; ramp through ~2032 | Through 2042 |

## The Acquisition Program: $7.25 Billion for 5.3 Gigawatts

The fiscal 2025 financial results were assembled on a portfolio that did not yet include the gas capacity acquired and agreed during the year. The $7.25 billion acquisition program represents the most consequential capital allocation decision in Talen's post-reorganisation history, and its logic is inseparable from the PJM capacity market dynamics that produced the $333.44 per megawatt-day clearing price.

The Freedom and Guernsey transaction — two natural gas combined-cycle facilities totalling 2.8 gigawatts — closed during fiscal 2025 at $3.8 billion, implying a transaction price of approximately $1,357 per kilowatt. For context, new-build gas combined-cycle capacity in PJM at comparable heat-rate specifications was being quoted in the $1,800 to $2,200 per kilowatt range during 2025, reflecting supply-chain constraints on turbines and balance-of-plant equipment. Acquiring operating facilities below new-build cost, in a market where new-build lead times stretch to seven years or more, is a form of scarcity arbitrage. Freedom and Guernsey immediately participate in the capacity market, earn energy margin, and require no permitting or interconnection queue risk.

The Cornerstone transaction, agreed but not closed at the snapshot date, adds 2.0 gigawatts of combined-cycle capacity and 456 megawatts of peaking capacity — 2,456 megawatts in total — for $3.45 billion, implying approximately $1,404 per kilowatt across the full package. The marginal premium over Freedom and Guernsey likely reflects competitive tension in the market for premium gas assets as other IPPs pursued similar consolidation strategies.

Taken together, the two transactions add approximately 5.3 gigawatts of gas capacity for $7.25 billion, raising the pro-forma fleet to roughly 18.4 gigawatts. The gas fleet, in the PJM capacity market context, is not merely a merchant earnings stream — it is a portfolio of capacity awards, each of which clears the annual auction and generates revenue before a single megawatt-hour of energy is dispatched.

## Capital Structure and the 3.5x Discipline

Funding a $7.25 billion acquisition program while maintaining investment-grade-adjacent leverage requires debt issuance at scale. Talen executed two senior unsecured notes offerings: $1.4 billion of 6.250% notes due 2034 and $1.3 billion of 6.500% notes due 2036, raising $2.7 billion of long-duration fixed-rate debt in a rate environment that had moved against issuers. The coupon levels — 6.25% and 6.50% — reflect the company's sub-investment-grade credit profile post-reorganisation, but the maturities of 2034 and 2036 provide a runway through which the contracted revenue layers and the gas acquisitions can season before refinancing risk materialises.

The remaining acquisition funding comes from a combination of adjusted free cash flow — $524 million in fiscal 2025 alone — and, where applicable, assumption of existing project-level debt. Management has stated a net leverage target of around 3.5 times or lower over the cycle, a formulation that signals acceptance of peak leverage above that level during the acquisition phase, with a path toward deleveraging as EBITDA grows. At $1,035 million of fiscal 2025 adjusted EBITDA, $2.7 billion of new notes issuance represents approximately 2.6 turns of incremental debt — manageable if the acquisition program delivers the EBITDA contribution embedded in transaction underwriting.

The 50% FCF-to-EBITDA conversion ratio is the mechanism through which deleveraging occurs without asset sales. At $524 million of adjusted free cash flow in fiscal 2025, the company generates, on an annualised basis, enough cash to retire roughly one-fifth of the new notes issuance in a single year if it directed all free cash toward debt reduction rather than further capital deployment.

## Operating Leverage: The Path to FY27-28

The financial architecture described above creates a specific kind of operating leverage. Susquehanna's cost structure — approximately $459 million in annual production costs — does not scale with revenue. Whether the plant earns merchant pricing in PJM or contracted Amazon PPA pricing, the fuel and operating cost base is essentially fixed. Each incremental dollar of contracted revenue above the cost basis flows nearly unimpaired to EBITDA.

As the Amazon PPA ramps from its current partial-volume delivery toward the 1,920-megawatt contracted ceiling by approximately 2032, and as Freedom, Guernsey, and Cornerstone contribute a full year's capacity revenue for the first time in the 2027/2028 delivery year, the revenue base will be substantially larger than what produced $1,035 million of adjusted EBITDA in fiscal 2025. The fixed-cost base of the nuclear and gas operations will not grow commensurately. The result — barring commodity price deterioration or operational setbacks — is a step-change in EBITDA that could move the metric materially higher by fiscal years 2027 and 2028.

That trajectory is the operating-leverage thesis that informed a $7.25 billion capital commitment and $2.7 billion of new debt in a single fiscal year. Talen's management and board — populated with veterans of Texas Competitive Electric Holdings, GenOn, Exelon, and Apollo — have navigated at least one full power-market cycle each. The bet they have made, expressed in capital structure and acquisition terms, is that the AI electricity demand wave sustains long enough for the contracted revenue architecture to compound, and that PJM's supply shortfall persists through the capacity auction cycles that determine whether the gas fleet earns its cost of capital.

chapters.title: From restructuring print to $1B EBITDA
chapters.body:
## The opening print: a company finding its footing

When Talen Energy re-listed on NASDAQ in 2023 as ticker TLN, the market's first task was to price a company with no public earnings history in its current form — a Pennsylvania nuclear and gas operator that had spent the prior year reorganising its capital structure through Chapter 11, emerging with a stripped balance sheet and an executive suite assembled from the most battle-hardened alumni of prior generation-sector restructurings. Mark McFarland, installed as chief executive in May 2023 after serving in similar post-restructuring CEO roles at California Resources Corporation, GenOn Energy, and Luminant, began his public tenure by articulating a thesis that most sell-side analysts had not yet built into their models: that Susquehanna, Talen's 2.5 GW boiling-water reactor complex in Salem Township, Pennsylvania, was an underpriced asset on a per-megawatt-hour basis and that the structural demand shift implied by hyperscaler data centre build-outs would eventually force that repricing.

The initial public earnings prints validated the merchant-power baseline. Susquehanna's operating economics were already compelling: at approximately $27 per MWh implied lifecycle cost, the plant generated roughly 17 TWh annually under Talen's 90% ownership share — competitive against virtually any dispatchable baseload source on the PJM interconnect. The fleet's early EBITDA trajectory reflected that nuclear cost advantage, offset by the inherent volatility of unhedged merchant exposure in a PJM power market that had not yet experienced the demand inflection that AI data centre construction would eventually deliver. The stock traded at a discount to replacement cost, consistent with how the market historically valued restructured IPPs before the next earnings catalyst arrived.

## The Amazon announcement and the re-rating event

That catalyst arrived on March 4, 2024, when Talen filed an 8-K disclosing an initial power purchase agreement with Amazon Web Services to supply nuclear-generated electricity from Susquehanna to Amazon's data centre campus in Salem Township — situated immediately adjacent to the plant. The structure was economically novel: rather than a financial hedge or a RECs-only arrangement, the initial agreement gave Amazon rights to carbon-free baseload power at a contracted price, delivered physically at or near the point of generation, without PJM transmission loss between generator and load. For an AI data centre operator with round-the-clock electricity appetite and a corporate sustainability commitment, it was functionally a utility contract in everything but regulatory name. [Talen Energy IR](https://ir.talenenergy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/talen-energy-expands-nuclear-energy-relationship-amazon)

The equity market's reaction was immediate and pronounced. TLN shares moved sharply higher on the 8-K filing date and sustained a significant portion of the gain as investors — many of them newly introduced to the AI-electricity infrastructure subsector through parallel coverage of Vistra, Constellation, and NRG — re-underwritten the Susquehanna asset value from PJM merchant price deck assumptions to hyperscaler-PPA contracted-price assumptions. The repricing logic was straightforward: a plant generating 17 TWh at $27/MWh all-in cost, previously valued against PJM power curves, now had a visible contracted counterparty willing to pay meaningfully more for long-duration, carbon-attributable, baseload delivery. The spread between $27/MWh production cost and the PPA contract price — undisclosed, as is standard in competitive PPA filings — constituted the margin that analysts began capitalising at a multiple more consistent with contracted utility cash flows than with merchant generation.

## Building the revenue architecture: RMR, PJM capacity, and acquisitions

Through the second half of 2024 and into 2025, Talen systematically added contracted revenue layers that reduced its dependence on unhedged spot-price exposure. The mechanics operated on three parallel tracks.

First, reliability-must-run contracts. PJM's grid operator designated Talen's Brandon Shores and H.A. Wagner plants in Maryland as reliability-critical units and mandated their continued operation through fixed-payment RMR contracts starting June 2025. Brandon Shores carries an annual payment of $145 million; H.A. Wagner adds $35 million — together $180 million of fixed annual revenue running through May 2029, independent of power prices. [Utility Dive](https://www.utilitydive.com/news/talen-amazon-aws-susquehanna-nuclear-data-centert/750440/)

Second, the PJM capacity market. In the 2027/2028 base residual auction, Talen cleared 8,745 MW at $333.44 per MW-day — the highest clearing price the PJM capacity market had seen in years, driven by the retirement of older coal capacity and accelerating load growth projections from data centre construction across the interconnect. At $333.44 per MW-day on 8,745 MW, the implied annual capacity payment stream from that auction result alone approaches $1.06 billion — a number that, layered against Susquehanna's merchant and PPA revenue, materially reshaped the earnings visibility profile.

Third, fleet expansion. The Freedom and Guernsey acquisition — 2.8 GW of natural gas combined-cycle capacity acquired for approximately $3.8 billion and closed during FY2025 — broadened the earnings base beyond nuclear into the gas-fired segment of PJM dispatch. Talen followed with the Cornerstone agreement at approximately $3.45 billion, adding a further 2.0 GW of combined-cycle and 456 MW of peaking capacity. Total gas-capacity additions from the two transactions: approximately 5.3 GW for $7.25 billion, financed in part by $1.4 billion of 6.250% senior unsecured notes due 2034 and $1.3 billion of 6.500% senior unsecured notes due 2036. Management communicated a target of net leverage around 3.5x or lower across the cycle — acknowledging that the acquisition program meaningfully increased gross debt while framing the capital structure as appropriate for the contracted-cash-flow quality of the expanded fleet.

## The 2025 quarterly progression

The 2025 calendar year saw each quarterly reporting cycle confirm that the contracted-revenue architecture was translating into durable earnings delivery. Second-quarter 2025 results, reported August 7, 2025, reflected Susquehanna's strong generation output under the AWS PPA's initial volume tranche alongside the first full-quarter contribution of the Freedom and Guernsey fleet. Third-quarter results, reported November 5, 2025, narrowed the full-year EBITDA guidance band as the operating trajectory became clearer, with management commentary focused on the pace of the Amazon delivery ramp and the integration cadence for the newly acquired gas assets.

In June 2025, Talen and Amazon announced the expansion of the PPA to up to 1,920 MW of carbon-free nuclear power through 2042 — with a ramp schedule projecting potential full-volume delivery by approximately 2032 and delivery rights extended to Amazon sites elsewhere in Pennsylvania beyond the Salem Township campus. The June expansion also incorporated an option for co-development of Small Modular Reactors within Talen's Pennsylvania footprint. That optionality carries no near-term revenue contribution but is analytically significant: it signals Amazon's appetite for a deeper, longer-duration electricity supply relationship with Talen, and frames the PPA not as a transactional hedge but as an infrastructure partnership spanning multiple nuclear technology generations. [Talen Energy IR](https://ir.talenenergy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/talen-energy-expands-nuclear-energy-relationship-amazon)

December 2025 brought a management realignment calibrated to the company's new scale. Terry Nutt, who had served as chief financial officer, was elevated to president, assuming operating oversight responsibility commensurate with a 13.1 GW multi-fuel fleet. Cole Muller, previously executive vice president for strategic ventures and the executive most closely associated with the Cornerstone negotiation, was named chief financial officer effective December 15, 2025. The succession was framed as an operational maturation rather than a leadership disruption — a formalisation of the division between fleet management and financial stewardship as the AWS delivery ramp and Cornerstone closing approached simultaneously.

## FY2025: $1,035 million and what it means

The fiscal year 2025 print, reported in February 2026, landed at $1,035 million of adjusted EBITDA and $524 million of adjusted free cash flow on the 13.1 GW fleet. The FCF-to-EBITDA conversion ratio of approximately 50% is notable for an IPP with meaningful maintenance capital expenditure obligations at a two-unit boiling-water reactor — it reflects the operating leverage inherent in Susquehanna's low variable-cost structure once fixed operating and maintenance costs are absorbed.

| Metric | FY2025 |
|---|---|
| Adjusted EBITDA | $1,035M |
| Adjusted FCF | $524M |
| FCF / EBITDA conversion | ~50% |
| Susquehanna generation | ~17 TWh |
| Susquehanna implied LCOE | ~$27/MWh |
| Total fleet capacity | 13.1 GW |
| RMR annual revenue (run-rate) | $180M |
| PJM 2027/28 capacity cleared | 8,745 MW at $333.44/MW-day |

The $1,035 million figure represents a materially different earnings quality than the restructuring-era merchant baseline. The components layering into adjusted EBITDA now include: Amazon PPA contracted revenue at Susquehanna; $180 million of fixed RMR payments from Brandon Shores and H.A. Wagner beginning June 2025; the capacity-market clearing revenue from 8,745 MW at the highest PJM auction price in years; and the initial earnings contribution from the Freedom and Guernsey fleet operating its first full year as a Talen subsidiary.

## A structurally different story

The cumulative observation that closes the earnings narrative is this: the post-restructuring Talen Energy is not the same commercial animal that filed Chapter 11. The company that emerged in 2023 was a Pennsylvania nuclear and gas merchant whose earnings were primarily exposed to PJM spot prices, weather, and the economics of dispatch relative to natural gas curves. The company that printed $1,035 million of adjusted EBITDA for FY2025 is defined by stacked contracted revenue — a multi-decade Amazon PPA anchoring the Susquehanna output, four years of fixed RMR payments on two Maryland fossil plants, and a 2027/2028 PJM capacity auction result that locks in approximately $1.06 billion of annual capacity payments on cleared megawatts at a price level the market had not seen in a generation.

That structural shift from merchant to contracted does not eliminate commodity exposure — gas price volatility still runs through the Freedom, Guernsey, and prospective Cornerstone combined-cycle units, and PJM energy market conditions still influence dispatch economics across the fleet. But it does mean that a growing proportion of Talen's EBITDA is now derivable from long-dated contracts with investment-grade counterparties, reducing the sensitivity of the earnings model to any single quarter's power prices. For a company that spent 2022 in bankruptcy, the architecture of the 2025 print is the most important single data point in the investment case.

chapters.title: McFarland, Schaefer, and the EFH+GenOn alumni cluster
chapters.body:
## The Restructuring Archetype at the Top

When Talen Energy's board recruited Mark "Mac" McFarland as chief executive in May 2023, they were not searching for a conventional utility operator. They were looking for a specific type of executive — one who had navigated the full lifecycle of a distressed US power company, from creditor negotiation through asset rationalisation to equity re-listing, and who understood the commercial architecture of merchant power well enough to reposition a company on the far side of that process. McFarland, 56, was the template.

His curriculum vitae reads as a guided tour through the most consequential restructurings in American power. He began at Exelon as a senior vice president, absorbing the operating and commercial discipline of the largest US nuclear operator. He moved to Energy Future Holdings — the former TXU, the $45bn leveraged buyout that became the largest corporate bankruptcy in US history — as chief commercial officer, where he managed the commodity exposure of a fleet that included Luminant's coal and gas generation across Texas. When EFH's restructuring separated Luminant, McFarland stayed as Luminant's chief commercial officer. He then served as executive chairman and chief executive of GenOn Energy, the competitive-generation subsidiary of NRG that itself entered bankruptcy in 2017. His final pre-Talen role was chief executive and president of California Resources Corporation, an oil and gas producer that also emerged from Chapter 11. The pattern is not incidental. McFarland has run the commercial operations of companies in financial stress and rebuilt them for re-listing. That experience — specifically the combination of deep power-markets fluency and creditor-cycle management — is precisely what Talen's board required when it emerged from its own Chapter 11 in May 2023, the same month McFarland joined.

His educational background reinforces the operational emphasis. A B.S. in civil engineering from Virginia Tech, an M.B.A. from the University of Delaware, and completion of MIT's Nuclear Reactor Technology Course form a credential stack unusual among IPP chief executives — engineering rigor at the foundation, commercial finance in the middle, and direct nuclear-reactor literacy at the top. For a company whose earnings architecture is anchored by a 2.5-gigawatt nuclear station supplying Amazon under a contract running to 2042, the nuclear-fluency component is not decorative.

## The EFH and GenOn Alumni Network

What makes Talen's executive team structurally distinctive is not any single hire but the density of Energy Future Holdings and GenOn alumni across both the management layer and the boardroom. This is not coincidence. EFH and GenOn produced a generation of power-markets professionals who were tested in ways that conventional regulated-utility careers do not replicate — negotiating with creditor committees, managing commodity books in distress, preserving asset value through bankruptcy proceedings, and then rebuilding commercial functions from the ground up. Talen's post-restructuring leadership is disproportionately drawn from that cohort.

Andrew Wright, 58, serves as chief administrative officer. His credential is specific: fourteen years as general counsel of Energy Future Holdings. Wright holds a B.B.A. in accounting from SMU, a J.D. from Notre Dame, and a CPA designation — a legal-and-accounting combination that reflects the administrative complexity of a multi-asset power company running through prolonged restructuring. He carries the deepest single EFH institutional memory on the executive team. Darren Olagues, 55, joined as chief development officer in October 2024, having served as CFO and senior advisor at GenOn Energy. His career also includes Cleco, Exelon, and Sithe Energies. He is the second GenOn alumnus in Talen's senior operating ranks, alongside McFarland.

On the board, the EFH thread runs through Anthony Horton, 65. Horton was chief financial officer of Energy Future Holdings and before that a senior director at TXU Energy. He holds a B.B.A. in economics from UT Arlington, a master's in professional accounting and finance from UT Dallas/Arlington, and carries the quadruple finance certifications of CPA, CFA, CMA, and CFM — a credential stack that is structurally rare for a single individual. As chair of Talen's compensation committee and a member of both the audit and risk oversight committees, Horton provides the board with direct pattern recognition of what EFH's commercial and financial architecture looked like from the inside, and how its analogues should be avoided or managed in Talen's own capital structure.

## The December 2025 Realignment

The management structure that McFarland assembled through 2023 and 2024 was reorganised materially in December 2025, when Talen announced what it described as a strategic realignment of its executive leadership. The two most consequential changes formalised a split that had been operationally emerging as the company's business model grew in complexity.

Terry Nutt, 49, was elevated to president effective 15 December 2025. Nutt holds a B.B.A. and an M.S. in accounting from Texas A&M and built his career across Vistra, EDF Trading, and Just Energy, where he served as chief financial officer. The Vistra pedigree is significant — Vistra is the largest competitive power producer in the US by generation capacity, and its finance culture reflects the operational discipline of a merchant generator operating across multiple electricity markets simultaneously. Nutt's elevation to president formalised his role as the principal operating counterpart to McFarland's strategic and external-facing function.

Cole Muller, 45, became chief financial officer on the same date. His credential is the most unusual on the senior team. He holds a commission from the US Naval Academy, an M.B.A. from Wharton, and a J.D. from the University of Pennsylvania — three institutions, three disciplines, each at the top of its category. Before entering the energy sector, he was an associate partner at McKinsey. At Talen, his prior titles were senior vice president for Cumulus Growth and executive vice president for strategic ventures — roles that positioned him as the internal architect of the company's data centre co-location thesis before it transacted. The inference is direct: the AWS power purchase agreement signed in March 2024 and expanded in June 2025, and the Cornerstone acquisition programme, were structured under Muller's intellectual ownership before he assumed the CFO title. Promoting the architect of a transaction into the role responsible for reporting its financial results is an organisational statement about continuity of ownership over the thesis.

## Nuclear Operations: Submarine Pedigree and Site Credentials

The nuclear operations layer of Talen's management reflects a standard but rigorous hiring pattern within the US civilian nuclear industry: executives who entered via US Navy submarine service and transitioned to commercial nuclear plant management carry a specific combination of technical competence, procedural discipline, and safety-culture formation that the Nuclear Regulatory Commission and plant operators regard as near-optimal preparation for senior site leadership.

Brad Berryman, 57, is chief operating officer. He completed US Navy submarine service before accumulating thirty years of nuclear plant management experience at Turkey Point in Florida, Wolf Creek in Kansas, and Palo Verde in Arizona — three of the largest nuclear installations in the US fleet — before joining Talen, where he previously served as chief nuclear officer. His B.S. in organisational management from Central Baptist College is secondary to the operational pedigree; the submarine commission and plant-management tenures are the credential that matters in nuclear operations hiring.

Edward Casulli, 56, is senior vice president and chief nuclear officer. He holds a B.S. in electrical engineering from the US Naval Academy and an executive master's in management of technology from the University of Pennsylvania. His most directly relevant prior role was site vice president at Susquehanna — the same two-unit boiling-water reactor complex now operating at approximately 90 percent Talen ownership and supplying Amazon's data centres under the 1,920-megawatt PPA. Casulli's operational fingerprints are on the specific facility whose performance now determines the reliability of Amazon's contracted carbon-free power supply through 2042.

## The Commercial and Legal Architecture

Chris Morice, 46, has served as chief commercial officer since 2023. His career traversed Lehman Brothers, EDF Trading, Topaz Power, and Koch Energy before arriving at Talen — a trajectory through investment banking, European utility trading, independent US generation, and commodity trading. The combination is appropriate for a CCO who must simultaneously manage PJM capacity-market positioning, RMR contract administration, and the commercial terms of a hyperscaler PPA.

Dale Lebsack, 50, chief asset development officer, joined Talen in 2015 via the acquisition of RJS Power. He holds a B.S. in mechanical engineering from Georgia Tech and previously served as chief fossil officer. His engineering background and prior Duke Energy and Entergy experience provide the asset-development function with the technical and siting discipline required for the gas-capacity acquisition programme.

John Wander, 58, general counsel and corporate secretary, brings thirty-two years of commercial law experience from Vinson & Elkins, where he was a shareholder litigation partner. The Texas energy-law credential at Vinson & Elkins — one of the premier energy-sector legal practices globally — is the appropriate background for counsel defending a hyperscaler-PPA contract architecture against potential regulatory challenge and managing the disclosure obligations of a newly re-listed NASDAQ company.

## Board Composition: Calibrated for the Cycle

Talen's seven-director board was not assembled to represent generic corporate governance best practice. Its composition reflects deliberate calibration for the specific governance challenges of a post-Chapter-11 independent power producer navigating a period of rapid sectoral change.

Stephen Schaefer, 62, chairs the board. His career at Riverstone Holdings — among the most consequential energy private equity firms in the US — combined with his board seats at GenOn Holdings, Golar LNG, TexGen Power, and Alpine Summit Energy Partners, and earlier work at Duke Energy North America, positions him as the restructuring-and-cycle-management chairman that Talen's governance structure requires. The B.S. in finance and accounting from Northeastern and the CFA designation underpin the financial-governance function.

Joseph Nigro, 61, chairs the risk oversight committee and sits on nominating and governance. His credentials are the most senior on the board in terms of operating scope: he was chief financial officer of Exelon and subsequently chief executive of Constellation Energy, the nuclear-generation subsidiary Exelon separated in 2022. He has completed the MIT Reactor Technology Course — the same programme on McFarland's CV — and currently serves as senior advisor to Blackstone's energy transition group, as chairman of Eos Energy Enterprises, and as a board member of Kindle Energy. His risk oversight chairmanship is where that combination of nuclear-operating, financial, and energy-transition credentials is deployed.

Karen Hyde, 64, chairs the audit committee. Her background is specifically suited to the nuclear-regulatory dimension of that role: she spent thirty years at Xcel Energy, retiring as senior vice president and chief compliance and ethics officer, and before joining Xcel worked as a nuclear engineer for the US Department of Defense. She holds a B.S. in metallurgical engineering from Lafayette College, an M.S. in mineral economics from the Colorado School of Mines, and a Certified Internal Auditor designation. The audit chair for a company whose principal earnings asset is a nuclear station subject to NRC oversight should understand nuclear regulatory compliance from engineering experience. Hyde does.

Gizman Abbas, 53, chairs the nominating and governance committee. His career arc — Southern Company, ExxonMobil, Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs, Apollo Global Management, and now founding principal of Direct Invest Development — combined with his current seat on the New York Independent System Operator board, provides the committee with both deep energy-markets knowledge and capital-markets transaction experience. The B.S. in electrical engineering from Auburn and the M.B.A. from Northwestern Kellogg bridge the technical and financial disciplines.

Christine Benson Schwartzstein, 45, is the youngest director and the longest-tenured Goldman Sachs investment banker on the board, having spent seventeen years in Goldman's investment banking division before moving to Orion Infrastructure Capital as managing director. She now sits on the boards of Apollo Infrastructure Company and Delek US Holdings. Her A.B. in earth and planetary sciences, magna cum laude, from Harvard is an unusual foundation for an infrastructure banker, but it reflects the scientific-and-quantitative depth that characterises the Goldman energy and infrastructure franchise. Her nominating and governance and risk oversight committee seats position her Goldman and Apollo Infrastructure experience where M&A execution and deal-structure governance intersect — precisely the functions under pressure as Talen completes the Freedom, Guernsey, and pending Cornerstone acquisitions.

The board's aggregate composition — a PE-and-restructuring chairman, an operating CEO from EFH and GenOn, an ex-Apollo and Goldman energy banker, an ex-EFH CFO with quadruple finance certifications, a retired Xcel SVP and DOD nuclear engineer as audit chair, the ex-Exelon CFO and ex-Constellation CEO as risk chair, and a seventeen-year Goldman banker now at Apollo Infrastructure on M&A governance — is structurally coherent. There is no separate independent technology director, an omission that is architecturally appropriate: Talen sells commodity baseload electricity to a hyperscaler, not technology to an enterprise. The governing competencies required are power-markets cycle management, nuclear-regulatory compliance, restructuring-legacy administration, and large-transaction execution. All seven board seats reflect one or more of those functions.

chapters.title: Amazon, PJM, RMR — the four-layer revenue stack
chapters.body:
## The PPA That Reset the Pricing Curve

When Amazon Web Services and Talen Energy disclosed the initial power purchase agreement in March 2024, the power sector spent the following weeks debating a single question: what price? The contract terms were not public, but the structure was legible enough. Talen was selling carbon-free baseload nuclear electricity from its Susquehanna steam electric station — a two-unit boiling water reactor on the North Branch Susquehanna River in Luzerne County, Pennsylvania — to Amazon's adjacent data center campus at rates set by hyperscaler demand rather than merchant market clearing. Susquehanna's all-in levelised cost of electricity, at approximately $27 per megawatt-hour against a fleet generating roughly 17 terawatt-hours annually in FY2025, is among the lowest-cost baseload profiles on the PJM grid. Whatever Amazon was paying above that cost floor, the spread represented a structural improvement in Talen's economics that no capacity auction could replicate.

The June 2025 expansion made the stakes explicit. The amended agreement extended the maximum contracted volume to [1,920 MW](https://ir.talenenergy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/talen-energy-expands-nuclear-energy-relationship-amazon) — effectively the totality of Susquehanna's output attributable to Talen's 90 percent ownership stake in the 2.5 GW station — with a term running through 2042 and a ramp schedule potentially reaching full volume by 2032. Delivery encompasses the Susquehanna-adjacent Amazon campus and other Pennsylvania sites. A co-development option for small modular reactors within Talen's Pennsylvania footprint was folded into the amended terms, extending the commercial relationship's theoretical horizon well beyond 2042.

The 1,920 MW figure is not incidental. It represents the largest single carbon-free data center power purchase agreement in US history by contracted volume, and it binds the output of a single nuclear facility to a single hyperscaler customer for nearly two decades. For Talen's revenue architecture, it transforms Susquehanna from a merchant baseload asset — exposed to PJM day-ahead and real-time price volatility — into something closer to a contracted utility: long tenor, carbon-free certification, fixed counterparty, AI-workload pricing. The contrast with the pre-bankruptcy Talen, which operated Susquehanna entirely into the PJM merchant market, is stark.

## The Capacity Market Underneath Everything

Below the Amazon PPA sits a second revenue layer that is structurally distinct and independently significant. PJM Interconnection, the regional transmission organisation covering 13 states and the District of Columbia, runs forward capacity auctions that commit generators to supply availability three years ahead. For the 2027/2028 delivery year, Talen cleared [8,745 MW at a price of $333.44 per megawatt-day](https://www.stocktitan.net/sec-filings/TLN/10-k-talen-energy-corp-files-annual-report-d8a48267db5f.html) — a clearing price that, applied across the committed volume, implies approximately $1.06 billion of annual capacity revenue at that price level.

The $333.44/MW-day figure is not a baseline; it represents a step-change uplift versus the capacity prices that prevailed across much of the 2018–2022 period, when PJM auctions repeatedly cleared at prices below $100/MW-day in many zones following the FERC-ordered Minimum Offer Price Rule disruptions and COVID-era demand contraction. The tightening of PJM's capacity market — driven by accelerating data center load growth, accelerated coal retirements, and generator retirements across the Mid-Atlantic — has compressing reserve margins in ways that structural capacity-market models underweighted. Talen's 8,745 MW clearing position captures that tightening across its nuclear, gas, and intermediate fleet simultaneously.

Capacity payments in PJM are paid for committed availability regardless of whether a plant actually dispatches. That feature makes them a near-fixed revenue stream against which capex and fixed operating cost can be planned. For a portfolio anchored by nuclear baseload — which earns both the capacity payment and the energy revenue simultaneously when dispatching — the combination of capacity revenue plus Amazon contract revenue plus wholesale energy revenue creates a layered stack at the same physical asset.

| Revenue Layer | Annual Run-Rate (est.) | Counterparty | Certainty |
|---|---|---|---|
| Amazon AWS PPA | Not disclosed (hyperscaler contract pricing) | Amazon.com Inc. | Contracted through 2042 |
| PJM Capacity — 2027/28 | ~$1.06B (at $333.44/MW-day × 8,745 MW) | PJM Interconnection | Cleared; delivery obligation |
| RMR — Brandon Shores + H.A. Wagner | $180M/year combined | PJM / MAAC/SWMAAC | Fixed through May 2029 |
| PJM Wholesale Energy | Merchant (varies with gas prices and load) | PJM day-ahead/real-time | Market-price dependent |

## RMR: The Grid's Insurance Premium

The third layer is the least intuitive for investors unfamiliar with PJM's reliability contracting. Reliability Must Run agreements — administered through PJM in coordination with FERC — are payments made to generators whose retirement would create transmission reliability violations in specific load pockets, even when those generators are uneconomic on a pure energy or capacity market basis. They are, in effect, an insurance premium paid by the grid to keep assets running that the market would otherwise shut down.

Talen's RMR portfolio covers two dual-fuel coal and oil plants in Maryland: Brandon Shores, a 1,305 MW facility on the Patapsco River in Anne Arundel County, and H.A. Wagner, a smaller peaking facility nearby. Both plants serve the MAAC and SWMAAC reliability zones — the Baltimore-Washington corridor load pocket that transmission constraints make difficult to serve purely through imports from other PJM zones. PJM awarded the RMR contracts effective June 2025, with fixed payments of [$145 million annually for Brandon Shores](https://ir.talenenergy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/talen-energy-expands-nuclear-energy-relationship-amazon) and $35 million annually for H.A. Wagner, both running through May 2029.

The combined $180 million per year is structurally guaranteed regardless of commodity prices, dispatch frequency, or broader market conditions. It is among the largest single RMR commitments in the PJM footprint. The economic logic for Talen is straightforward: plants that would otherwise have been candidates for retirement — with their fixed costs unsupported by merchant energy and capacity revenue at current prices — become fixed-revenue assets for four years, contributing meaningfully to the $1,035 million of adjusted EBITDA that the company reported for FY2025.

The RMR horizon matters. May 2029 is not a distant terminus; it coincides approximately with the period when Talen's Cornerstone acquisition is expected to have closed and its gas combined-cycle fleet will have been substantially integrated. The RMR payments provide cash flow bridge through a period of significant balance-sheet activity and acquisition integration.

## The Fourth Layer: Merchant Energy and the Gas Fleet

The fourth revenue layer — wholesale energy sales into PJM day-ahead and real-time markets — is the most variable and the most leveraged to commodity price movements. Nuclear generation from Susquehanna, which runs at high capacity factors year-round and has near-zero marginal cost, dispatches into PJM whenever the plant is available, earning market-clearing electricity prices set by the marginal generator on the system (typically natural gas). In high-price hours, Susquehanna earns outsized merchant revenue in addition to its Amazon PPA base.

The gas fleet adds dispatchability to the merchant layer. The $3.8 billion acquisition of Freedom and Guernsey, which closed during FY2025 and added approximately 2.8 GW of natural gas combined-cycle capacity, expands Talen's ability to capture PJM energy price spikes during periods of peak demand or nuclear outages. The agreed Cornerstone acquisition — approximately 2.0 GW of combined-cycle and 456 MW of peaking capacity at a transaction value of $3.45 billion — extends that dispatchable position further. Combined, the two transactions add roughly 5.3 GW of gas generation for approximately $7.25 billion of total consideration, funded in part through $2.7 billion of new senior unsecured debt (the $1.4 billion 6.250% notes due 2034 and the $1.3 billion 6.500% notes due 2036).

The gas build-out serves the Amazon relationship as much as the merchant market. Carbon-free delivery from Susquehanna to Amazon's Pennsylvania campus is the primary obligation under the PPA, but the broader contractual structure contemplates delivery across multiple Amazon Pennsylvania sites. Gas capacity provides firming capability — dispatchable generation that can backstop delivery obligations when Susquehanna is in planned refuelling outages or forced outages. Nuclear plants typically schedule refuelling outages every 18 to 24 months; during those windows, without dispatchable backup, a PPA counterparty faces delivery risk.

## Competitive Positioning Across the IPP Universe

The four-layer stack is not standard equipment for listed independent power producers. Constellation Energy, the largest US nuclear IPP by capacity and Talen's most direct comparable, has pursued its own data center PPA programme and cleared significant capacity in PJM auctions, but its nuclear fleet is spread across multiple states under different cost structures and its RMR exposure is limited. Vistra Corp operates a mixed nuclear and gas fleet with material Texas ERCOT exposure that dilutes its PJM capacity revenue concentration. NRG Energy's IPP portfolio is weighted toward retail electricity and gas-fired generation without a nuclear anchor. PSEG and Exelon are regulated utility holding companies whose earnings are rate-regulated rather than market-priced — a fundamentally different risk profile.

What distinguishes Talen's stack is simultaneity: the Amazon PPA, the PJM capacity auction clearing, the RMR contracts, and the merchant energy layer are all operating at material scale at the same time, layered atop each other at the same underlying generation assets. Susquehanna alone earns capacity revenue (from the PJM auction), energy revenue (from merchant dispatch), and PPA revenue (from Amazon) — three separate payment streams from a single physical unit. The RMR plants at Brandon Shores and H.A. Wagner earn their $180 million of fixed payments independently, with their own PJM capacity positions on top.

The structural observation that follows is not a marginal one. Few independent power producers in the listed universe have assembled a revenue stack with contracted multi-decade tenor at hyperscaler-buyer pricing, fixed RMR payments guaranteed by a regional grid operator, a forward-cleared capacity position at record auction prices, and a growing dispatchable gas fleet for merchant and firming upside — simultaneously, at a combined fleet scale exceeding 13 GW. Talen's FY2025 adjusted free cash flow of $524 million against adjusted EBITDA of $1,035 million — a 50 percent FCF conversion ratio unusual for a capital-intensive generation fleet — suggests that the stack is not merely theoretical. It is producing cash. The question sophisticated investors are pricing is how durable each layer is across the cycle: whether PJM capacity prices hold at elevated levels through the late 2020s, whether Amazon's data centre expansion sustains the implied electricity demand driving PPA pricing, and whether the gas acquisition programme can be integrated at the implied returns without eroding the balance sheet discipline that management has signalled with a net leverage target of approximately 3.5 times or lower over the cycle.

chapters.title: Where Talen sits in the AI electricity landscape
chapters.body:
